objective:
【研究命题·纯机器学习/数学】

解空间刚性 = 满足全部解析约束的函数集合的维数：低维/唯一 = 刚，高维/连续族 = 胖。

核心问题：小型前馈网络的“泛化行为”能否作为 bootstrap 解空间刚性的探针？
令 w = 约束样本数，N_c(w) = 在未参与训练的留出约束点上取得“零违规”所需的最小网络容量（用隐藏层宽度度量）。

【唯一硬性口径（不可更改，其余全由你决定）】
- 零违规 = 留出约束点上的最大绝对误差 ≤ 1e-3。
- 刚性 = 扫描范围内存在较小的有限 N_c（且 N_c 不随 w 增长）；胖 = 扫描上限内任何宽度都达不到零违规（N_c 不可达）。判别是二值的。
- 所有报告数值必须是有限数（禁止 inf/nan/None）。
- 研究对象只能是小型前馈网络本身。严禁把本命题替换或“换名归约”为材料/化学/玻璃/合金/离子导电等任何物理体系，也不要用别的领域类比回答。

【实验的族、样本、扫描、脚本如何设计，以及如何证明“刚性可达”，由你自己决定并给出理由。】

所有结论必须来自真实运行的可复现数值实验：给出扫描设置、训练与留出误差数值、以及 N_c(w) 的数值与趋势。

input_params.description: Implement a controlled numerical experiment to test the geometric hypothesis on solution-space rigidity using small feedforward networks. The script will: (1) Define a constraint function f(x) with known analytic properties; (2) Generate w training samples; (3) Train networks with varying hidden widths N; (4) Measure max absolute error on a held-out validation set; (5) Determine N_c(w) as the minimal width achieving zero violation (error ≤ 1e-3). The experiment will sweep w from 5 to 50 and N from 2 to 100, logging training/validation errors and N_c values. Results will be analyzed for rigidity (finite N_c constant in w) vs. fatness (N_c diverges or is unattainable).
input_params.expected_prediction: N_c(w) will be small (≤ 20) and roughly constant or sublinear in w for the tested range, indicating solution-space rigidity. If N_c grows rapidly or exceeds 100, the system is "fat".

input_params.description: Design and execute a numerical experiment to test the "geometry" hypothesis regarding solution space rigidity in small feedforward networks. Specifically: (1) define a family of analytic constraints (e.g., polynomial or trigonometric functions with known smoothness); (2) sample w constraint points; (3) sweep hidden layer width N from 4 to 64; (4) train network to minimize loss on training set; (5) evaluate max absolute error on held-out validation set; (6) record N_c(w) as minimum width achieving zero violation (error ≤ 1e-3); (7) repeat for multiple w values to assess scaling. Use standard activation (ReLU/Tanh), Adam optimizer, and sufficient training iterations to convergence. Plot N_c(w) vs w and assess whether N_c remains bounded (rigid) or grows unbounded (fat). Validate against literature on neural network capacity and Kolmogorov width.
input_params.expected_prediction: N_c(w) will remain small (≤16) and roughly constant or sublinear in w across tested range, indicating solution space rigidity; if N_c grows rapidly or saturates at high width, hypothesis may be falsified.

input_params.description: Design a bootstrap experiment to probe solution space rigidity of small feedforward networks. Generate an analytic constraint function (e.g., a polynomial or trigonometric function) with known properties. Sweep constraint sample size w and hidden layer width N. For each (w, N) pair, train a small feedforward network on w points, evaluate maximum absolute error on a held-out test set of constraints. Record N_c(w) = minimum N achieving max error ≤ 1e3. Plot N_c vs w to determine if rigidity (bounded N_c) holds. Use fixed random seeds for reproducibility.
input_params.expected_prediction: N_c(w) will remain small (≤16) and roughly constant or sublinear in w across the tested range, indicating solution space rigidity. If N_c grows rapidly or becomes infeasible, the space is "fat".

input_params.description: Implement a numerical experiment to test the phase-transition scaling hypothesis for minimal network capacity N_c(w) as a function of constraint density w. The experiment will: (1) Define a bootstrap constraint problem using a target function with known analytical constraints; (2) Systematically vary w (constraint count) and N (hidden layer width); (3) Train small feedforward networks to satisfy constraints; (4) Measure N_c(w) as the minimum width achieving zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3) on held-out constraints; (5) Analyze scaling behavior to identify rigid vs. fat regimes and critical w_c. The code will generate the required scan data, training/validation metrics, and N_c(w) values for analysis.
input_params.expected_prediction: The experiment will reveal a critical constraint density w_c below which N_c(w) remains constant (rigid regime, e.g., N_c ≈ 8-16) and above which N_c(w) grows rapidly (fat regime). The transition will appear as a sharp increase in N_c(w) at w_c. For w < w_c, networks of modest width achieve zero violation; for w > w_c, even large widths may fail to achieve zero violation within training budget, indicating N_c is effectively unbounded (fat). The exact w_c and scaling exponent will be determined from the scan results.

Analyze the scaling behavior: if N_c(w) saturates at a finite value below w_c, this supports the phase transition hypothesis; if N_c(w) grows or remains unbounded, the solution space is "fat". For w > w_c, N_c(w) will increase sharply or remain unbounded, indicating a fat phase. The critical density w_c will be identified as the point where N_c(w) begins to grow significantly.

input_params.description: Design and execute a bootstrap experiment to test if small feedforward networks act as probes of solution space rigidity. Train small feedforward networks with hidden width $N \in [8, 256]$ and measure $N_c(w)$ — the minimum width achieving max absolute error $\le 10^{-3}$ on held-out constraints. Scan $w \in [10, 200]$ to observe if $N_c$ remains bounded (rigid) or diverges (fat). Use symbolic regression on the recovered solution to identify functional form, validating against the ground-truth polynomial.
input_params.expected_prediction: For polynomial target functions, $N_c(w)$ will remain small and bounded ($N_c < 32$) across all tested $w$, indicating the solution space is rigid and networks efficiently capture the underlying structure without requiring excessive width as constraint density increases.

input_params.description: Reformulate the hypothesis to test the rigidity of the solution space rather than interpolation capacity. We will generate polynomial identity constraints with a known dual constraint matrix rank $r$, train a network with width $w$, and measure the dimension of the solution space (number of free parameters after constraints) as a function of $w$. The prediction is that for $w \geq r$, the solution space dimension saturates, indicating algebraic rigidity independent of further width increase. This avoids the interpolation contradiction by measuring structural capacity rather than fitting error.
input_params.expected_prediction: The solution space dimension (number of independent parameters satisfying constraints) will plateau when $w \geq r$, confirming that the constraint rank $r$ limits the effective degrees of freedom regardless of network width beyond saturation.

N_c(w) will saturate at a small constant value (e.g., N_c ≈ 8-16) independent of w for w above a threshold (~10-20), confirming the hypothesis that minimal capacity is determined by the intrinsic dimensionality of the constraint manifold rather than the number of constraints.
